query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an optimized heat treatment to induce a controlled precipitation of nanoscale, coherent intermetallic phases (analogous to a gamma-prime phase) in a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high‐entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance compared to the untreated homogeneous solid-solution alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high‐entropy alloy containing at least five elements in similar atomic percentages (5–35 at% each) produced by standard melting or additive manufacturing methods to yield a largely homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: A two‐step heat treatment consisting of a high-temperature solution treatment followed by an optimized aging step (for example, aging in the range of 700–900 °C for a few hours under an inert atmosphere) designed to precipitate nanoscale, coherent intermetallic (gamma’-like) phases.
generation.conditions: Solution treatment at a temperature high enough to homogenize the alloy (e.g., near the upper limit of the solid-solution stability) followed by aging at approximately 700–900 °C for 2–4 hours in an inert (argon) atmosphere; subsequent mechanical testing conducted at elevated temperatures (e.g., 800–1000 °C) to assess yield strength and creep performance.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of uniformly distributed nanoscale precipitates coherently embedded within the primary solid-solution matrix, which act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening whereby the precipitates pin dislocations and help suppress creep and plastic deformation at high temperatures, thereby increasing yield strength and mechanical stability under service conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast, single-phase alloy, the heat-treated alloy will show a statistically significant increase in yield strength and slower creep rates at elevated temperature due to the effective impediment of dislocation motion by the precipitates.
generation.baseline: Titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high‐entropy alloy in the untreated (as-cast or conventionally processed) homogeneous solid-solution state without significant secondary precipitate formation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to alloys with constituent element concentrations between 5 and 35 at% and operating at elevated temperatures below the precipitate dissolution limit (likely up to around 1000–1200 °C); outside these boundaries, either the precipitates may coarsen or dissolve, reducing the strengthening effect.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aging temperature/time and the exact precipitate volume fraction and coherence are not yet known and may need fine-tuning; there is also uncertainty about the long-term thermal stability of the induced precipitates under service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the titanium‐ and nickel‐primary HEA: one produced as-cast (or via a baseline processing without the specialized heat treatment) and a second subjected to the proposed two-step heat treatment (solution treatment followed by aging at 700–900 °C for 2–4 hours). Use microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM and XRD) to confirm the presence of nanoscale precipitates in the treated samples. Then perform mechanical tests such as high-temperature tensile or creep tests (at 800–1000 °C) on both sample sets.
measurements: Creep rate under constant load at elevated temperature
Precipitate size, distribution, and phase identification via TEM/XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the heat-treated specimens do not show a statistically significant improvement in yield strength or creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the untreated baseline, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal a meaningful difference in precipitate formation between the two sample sets.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as alloys that are composed of more than 4 elements with near equi-atomic percentage [,,,]. Due to their high mixing entropy, HEAs tend to form simple solid-solution phases, such as face-centered-cubic (FCC) [,], body-centered-cubic (BCC) [,,], and hexagonal-close-packed (HCP) structures [,]. With the entropic stabilization of solid-solution phases, HEAs have attracted significant attention, because of their outstanding properties at elevated temperatures, which results from severe lattice distortion and microstructural stability at high temperatures [,,]. Many refractory HEAs (RHEAs), which mainly consist of BCC-type single solid-solution phase, have been developed and investigated due to their excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures []. The excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures in RHEAs are significantly associated with their unique atomic structures (distorted lattices) and high melting temperatures of the constitutive refractory elements (Ti, Nb, V, Mo, Ta, W, and Cr) [,,,].
